title: The Code Room and the Black Chamber: Worthington, New York, Chungking, Ottawa
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Worthington, birth on the railroad line
stops.date_confidence: attested. Wikipedia, 'Herbert Yardley', gives the birth at Worthington, Indiana, 13 April 1889, corroborated by the NSA biographical listing. The coordinate is corrected to the town point, 39.1208/-86.9811, taken from en.wikipedia 'Worthington, Indiana'; the research pool carried 39.1225/-86.9758, about 500 m east-northeast of it. The father's trade, the mother's death, the 1905 church membership and the family address at 127 West Union Street are [R], carried by the pool from David Kahn, The Reader of Gentlemen's Mail, and confirmed by no source reached.
stops.campa: Herbert Osborn Yardley is born in Worthington, a Greene County railroad town on the White River, second of four children of Robert Kirkbride Yardley, station agent and telegrapher. The father teaches the son Morse at the key, and the son will spend his working life on the far side of that skill, reading messages meant for other men. His mother dies when he is thirteen. At sixteen he joins the town's Presbyterian church. The house is remembered locally at 127 West Union Street, an address no record reached here confirms.

stops.name: Denver, the freight trains west
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The pool carries the freight-riding trip and the bartending from Kahn's biography; no source fetched this session confirms either, and no day within May is given, so 01 is a default. The coordinate is a general Denver point, not a boarding house or a bar.
stops.campa: At seventeen he rides freight west out of Indiana, comes into Denver with nothing, tends bar for a season and goes home. He makes part of the same run again the following year. Nothing in the trip is criminal and nothing in it is respectable: it is a boy from a railroad town using the railroad the way it is easiest to use, riding in the empty cars his father's timetables governed. The bar work is the first of many jobs he takes that have no bearing on what he is good at. Kahn's biography is the only account of either trip, and it fixes no day, no boarding house and no bar.
suggested_refs: Kahn's account of the two western trips of 1906 and 1907

stops.name: Worthington High School, the flag and the refused apology
stops.date_confidence: [R], and directly contradicted by the source the pool cites elsewhere. Wikipedia, fetched verbatim, states: 'After graduation from high school in 1907, Yardley went to the University of Chicago, but dropped out after one year.' It records an ordinary graduation at Worthington and says nothing of a flag, a suspension or a transfer. The expulsion narrative is Kahn's, relayed by the pool and unconfirmed here. Both versions are carried; neither is adjudicated. Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01 January.
stops.campa: A prank with the school flag ends in a demand for an apology, and the boy will not give it. The suspension is made permanent. He is by every account quick at mathematics and quicker at cards, and the town's verdict on him hardens early into a shape it keeps: gifted, unbiddable, not sorry. What was actually done to the flag no reachable source describes. Kahn's biography carries the episode whole; the capsule accounts say only that he graduated here in 1907 and went on to Chicago.

sources: David Kahn, The Reader of Gentlemen's Mail, per the research pool

stops.name: Eaton Rapids, the schooling finished away from home
stops.date_confidence: [R] for Eaton Rapids, [A] for the university year. The Michigan schooling is Kahn's, via the pool, unconfirmed here. The University of Chicago year and its abandonment after one year are attested by Wikipedia. Coordinate corrected to the town point 42.5092/-84.6533 from en.wikipedia 'Eaton Rapids, Michigan'; the pool carried 42.5084/-84.6605, roughly 600 m west. Day within June unknown, defaulted.
stops.campa: He finishes his secondary schooling at Eaton Rapids in Michigan, three hundred miles from the town that suspended him, and in the autumn enters the University of Chicago. He lasts a year and leaves. What he studied there, and why he stopped, is in no source reached. Every formal education he will ever have is now behind him: a school certificate earned twice over and a single abandoned university year. The cryptology he becomes known for he teaches himself, at night, off other people's telegrams.

stops.name: Indianapolis Union Station, the telegrapher's key
stops.date_confidence: [R] for the Indianapolis posting, [A] for the 1912 examination and appointment. The pool gives the railroad telegraphy at several Indiana points as Kahn's, undated within 1907-1912; 1909 is an ordering date and the day is a default. The coordinate is corrected to 39.7631/-86.1594, the station at 350 South Illinois Street per en.wikipedia 'Indianapolis Union Station'; the pool carried 39.7647/-86.1733, about 1.2 km west of it and across the river channel. The civil service examination and the State Department clerkship are attested by Wikipedia.
stops.campa: He works the railroad wires at points around Indiana, Indianapolis among them, taking and sending Morse for a living at the trade his father taught him. The work is exact and dull, and it trains the ear that matters later: a man who has spent years hearing sense inside a stream of clicks does not find it strange that meaning can be pulled out of a stream of anything. In 1912 he sits the federal civil service examination and passes. Washington offers him a clerkship in the State Department code room at nine hundred dollars a year.

stops.name: The State Department code room, the oath at nine hundred dollars
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the appointment: Wikipedia has Yardley passing the civil service examination and hired as a State Department code clerk in 1912. The precise day, 23 December, and the salary figure are the pool's, from Kahn, and unconfirmed here. The coordinate is the State, War and Navy Building at 17th Street and Pennsylvania Avenue NW, where the department was then housed; the identification is the pool's and is standard for the period.
stops.campa: He takes the oath as a code clerk in the old State, War and Navy Building at Seventeenth Street and Pennsylvania Avenue, twenty-three years old, and begins encoding and decoding the cables of American diplomacy. The codes are old. Some are decades old. The other clerks handle them the way clerks handle any office system, without asking what a foreign government with a copyist and a month of evenings might do to them. Yardley asks. He is the only man in the room treating the codebook as a problem rather than as furniture.
stops.quote: At that time I knew exactly nothing about the solution of the diplomatic codes and ciphers of foreign nations.
stops.quote_source: Herbert O. Yardley, The American Black Chamber (Bobbs-Merrill, 1931), Chapter I, p. 17

stops.name: Washington, the marriage to Hazel Milam
stops.date_confidence: [R] throughout. The marriage, the date, the ages and the venue at the home of the Reverend James H. Taylor are the pool's, from Kahn, and are confirmed by no source fetched this session; the Reno divorce of 28 August 1944 is [R] from the same source. The street address of the Taylor house is unestablished, so the coordinate is a general Washington point, not the house. The couple's address at 1009 Seventh Street NE is likewise [R].
stops.campa: Herbert Yardley and Hazel Milam, both twenty-five, marry at the Washington home of the Reverend James H. Taylor. They set up at 1009 Seventh Street Northeast, a rowhouse in the blocks behind the Capitol, on a clerk's pay. The marriage runs thirty years and ends in a Nevada courtroom on a sworn statement of residence that was not true. Whether any of it was happy is not recorded anywhere reached. Kahn is the only source for the wedding, and the Taylor house has never been located to a street, so the point here is the city and not the parlor they stood in.

stops.name: The code room, the cable to Wilson solved in two hours
stops.date_confidence: [A] for the episode, [R] for the date. Yardley's own Chapter I describes copying a 500-word coded telegram from Colonel Edward M. House to President Wilson off the wire the State Department shared with the White House, and solving it in under two hours; the quotation is verbatim from the 1931 text, pp. 21-22. Neither he nor any source reached dates it. 1915 orders the segment inside his 1912-1917 clerkship and the day is a default. The pool's own note that this was a foreign cipher is wrong: the code was American.
stops.campa: Working the night watch, he copies off the wire a five-hundred-word coded telegram from Colonel Edward House to President Wilson, passing over the line the department shares with the White House. It is an American code, guarding the president's own correspondence. He solves it in under two hours. What follows is not triumph but a kind of dread: if a clerk on a night shift can do this with what is already in his desk, then nothing the United States government sends has a floor under it. He tells nobody who is in a position to act.
stops.quote: Imagine my amazement when I was able to solve the message in less than two hours!
stops.quote_source: Herbert O. Yardley, The American Black Chamber (1931), Chapter I, pp. 21-22
suggested_refs: The shared State Department and White House telegraph line over which the House cable passed
sources: Herbert O. Yardley, The American Black Chamber (1931), Chapter I (archive.org, american-black-chamber-ii-watermark)

stops.name: Washington, the weakness nobody wants told
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to date and as to any single occasion. The quotation and the judgment behind it are verbatim from The American Black Chamber, Chapter I, pp. 20 and 22, but Yardley narrates them as the conclusion of his clerkship years rather than of one day. 1916 is an ordering date within 1912-1917; the day is a default. Nothing reached this session records what he submitted, to whom, or what answer he got.
stops.campa: The conclusion he reaches at the desk is not about any one message. It is that the United States protects its diplomacy with systems a determined amateur can break in an evening, and that no one whose business it is has checked. He is a clerk of twenty-six with no standing to say so and he says so anyway, in memoranda that go up and stop. The war in Europe is two years old and every belligerent is reading somebody, and the department goes on cabling in codes compiled before he was born. What he wrote in those memoranda, who read them and what answer came back is in nothing reached; the papers themselves have turned up in no archive.
stops.quote: Is it possible that a man sits in the White House, dreaming, picturing himself a maker of history, an international statesman, a mediator of peace, and sends his agents out with schoolboy ciphers?
stops.quote_source: Herbert O. Yardley, The American Black Chamber (1931), Chapter I, p. 22
suggested_refs: Yardley's memoranda on the insecurity of American diplomatic codes, 1915-1917, not located in any archive reached
sources: Herbert O. Yardley, The American Black Chamber (1931), Chapter I (archive.org, american-black-chamber-ii-watermark)

stops.name: Washington, the commission and the eighth section
stops.date_confidence: attested as to date and post: Wikipedia, verbatim, 'In June 1917, Yardley became a 2nd lieutenant in the Signal Corps and head of the newly created eighth section of military intelligence, MI-8.' The rank is second lieutenant; the pool twice wrote first lieutenant against its own cited source, and that error is corrected here. The Black Chamber article adds the assignment date of 5 July 1917 with 'Yardley and two civilian clerks'. The figure of about 151 staff by November 1918 is [R], present in the pool and in no source reached. The coordinate is an acknowledged general Washington placeholder: no source reached names the MI-8 building. The Shepherd Street NE address is [R], from Kahn.
stops.campa: In June he is commissioned a second lieutenant in the Signal Corps and given the eighth section of military intelligence, MI-8, which on the day he is assigned to lead it consists of himself and two civilian clerks. Ralph Van Deman, building an intelligence division out of nothing, has taken the code clerk's argument seriously where the State Department did not. Yardley moves the household out to 542 Shepherd Street Northeast in Brookland and starts hiring: linguists, mathematicians, a professor of English philology, women out of the universities.
stops.quote: Take this note to Colonel Gibbs and tell him I said to get your commission through at the earliest possible moment. Can you start Monday?
stops.quote_source: Ralph Van Deman to Yardley, Washington, 1917, quoted in Herbert O. Yardley, The American Black Chamber (1931), Chapter I

stops.name: Washington, the Witzke cryptogram
stops.date_confidence: attested that MI-8 under Yardley helped solve the coded cryptogram taken from the arrested German agent Lothar Witzke (Wikipedia). Month and day are not given anywhere reached and August is an ordering date. The arrest was in the US-Mexico border region; the solution was done in Washington, and the stop is placed where the work happened rather than where the arrest did. The coordinate is the same general Washington placeholder as the MI-8 stop.
stops.campa: A German agent arrested near the Mexican border is carrying a coded message nobody can read. It comes to MI-8, and the section takes it apart: the solution identifies Lothar Witzke as a German naval officer and saboteur, and it is read into a military commission that sentences him to death. It is the only such conviction the American war produces, and it comes not from an informant or a raid but from men at desks with pencils and frequency counts. The clerk's argument of 1915 has now been demonstrated against somebody else's code.
suggested_refs: The Witzke cryptogram and its solution by MI-8, entered in evidence at the 1918 military commission
sources: Wikipedia, 'Herbert Yardley'

stops.name: The Ritz Hotel, London, kept out of Room 40
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The London mission, the Ritz, the move to cheaper lodging and the exclusion from Room 40's most sensitive naval work are the pool's, from Kahn, unconfirmed by anything fetched this session. The date within 1918 is an ordering date; no month or day is recorded anywhere reached. The coordinate is the Ritz at Piccadilly.
stops.campa: Sent across to learn how the British do the work, he lands in a London where the trade is thirty years older than his own. He puts up at the Ritz, finds the bill impossible on his pay and moves to cheaper rooms. The War Office shows him method and technique. Room 40, the Admiralty office that read the Zimmermann telegram, he is kept away from. Allies exchange courtesies; they do not exchange their best material, and he never accepts it as a rule even after he has learned it. Was he told a reason, or simply steered past the door? Nothing reached says.
suggested_refs: Room 40, the Admiralty cryptanalytic office, from which the American visitor was excluded
sources: David Kahn, The Reader of Gentlemen's Mail, per the research pool

He is twenty-nine, running a bureau, and out of the United States for the second time in his life. His own account of these months keeps a dancer named Jacqueline in it, and no other document does. What he is doing officially is watching a conference in which decoded correspondence is one of the instruments on the table.

stops.name: Paris, the peace conference and the argument he brings home
stops.date_confidence: [R] as to Yardley's own activity: his presence and work at the Paris negotiations is the pool's, from Kahn, not independently confirmed. The date is an ordering date within the conference. The coordinate is the canonical Paris pin, 48.8566/2.3522, inherited byte-identical as the corpus carries it in arthur_balfour.journey.json and chaim_weizmann.journey.json; it is a city pin and not a room.
stops.campa: Through the negotiations he sees the political use of read correspondence at close range: delegations arguing positions their opponents have already read in clear. The French analysts he meets work for a service that has never once been disbanded between wars. That is the argument he carries home and puts to Washington that spring, a bureau kept standing in peacetime, paid for by the Army and the State Department together, reading foreign traffic while there is no war on. In May they agree to fund it.

stops.name: New York, the Code Compilation Company
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia has the Army and State Department jointly funding a peacetime Cipher Bureau with operations moved to New York and Yardley as director, and the Black Chamber article gives the move date as 20 May 1919 and the cover as the Code Compilation Company. The pool wrote 'Code Compiling Company', which its own cited source contradicts; corrected here. Charles Mendelsohn's co-ownership is [R], in the pool and in no source reached. The precise street address is unestablished, sometimes given as East 38th Street; the coordinate is an acknowledged Midtown placeholder.
stops.campa: On the twentieth of May the bureau moves to New York, funded jointly by the Army and the State Department, and hangs out the sign of the Code Compilation Company, a firm that compiles commercial codes for businesses and does so, in fact, at a profit. Behind the cover, some twenty people read the diplomatic traffic of foreign governments off cables the American telegraph companies hand over without a warrant. The name the bureau acquires later, and gives to a book, is the American Black Chamber. Yardley is thirty and directs it from an address no source reached establishes, East 38th Street being the one sometimes given.

stops.name: Memorial Continental Hall, the Washington Naval Conference
stops.date_confidence: attested for the conference and the decrypts: the US State Department Office of the Historian confirms the conference at Washington under Secretary Hughes and the 5:5:3 ratio, and the pool has the Black Chamber solving Japanese diplomatic traffic and passing translations to American officials during the talks. The venue is Memorial Continental Hall, 1776 D Street NW, per en.wikipedia, which states the building 'was the site of the Washington Naval Conference in 1921-22'; the pool inverted the name to 'Continental Memorial Hall' and pinned 38.8951/-77.0412, about 170 m off. Corrected to 38.8939/-77.0400. November 1921 is the opening; the day here is a default. Kahn's caveat, that Japan accepted the ratio on 12 December 1921 before some celebrated decrypts arrived, is [R] and unverified here.
stops.campa: Delegations from five nations sit at Memorial Continental Hall on D Street to divide the world's capital ships by ratio. Yardley's bureau is reading Tokyo's instructions to its own delegation and passing translations to Secretary of State Charles Evans Hughes, who negotiates knowing the floor below which the Japanese are authorized to concede. The conference ends at five to five to three. Kahn's reconstruction complicates the legend of the single decisive telegram: Japan accepted the ratio on the twelfth of December 1921, and some of the famous decrypts arrive after that.

stops.name: Washington, the Distinguished Service Medal
stops.date_confidence: attested. The pool tagged this [R] as unverifiable; it is confirmed independently at valor.militarytimes.com, hero record 18395, which prints the full citation to Major (Signal Corps) Herbert O. Yardley under War Department General Orders No. 56 (1922), for service 'as Chief of the Communication Section of the Military Intelligence Division, War Department General Staff'. Note the citation's own wording is Communication Section, not MI-8. No day within 1922 is given, so 01 January is a default. The tuberculosis and the Arizona recuperation are [R], from Kahn via the pool, with no town established.
stops.campa: The War Department awards him the Distinguished Service Medal as Major, Signal Corps, for wartime service as Chief of the Communication Section of the Military Intelligence Division. The citation names no cipher and no solved message; it names a duty of great responsibility, which is what such orders say about work that cannot be printed in them. The same year the strain of the conference tells and he spends months in Arizona with a mild tuberculosis before going back to the bureau.

stops.name: Astoria, the Queens lots
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The real estate investment through Cody Realty, in Astoria, Woodside and Jackson Heights, is the pool's, from Kahn, unconfirmed by anything fetched this session. The pool dates it only to the 1920s; 1926 is an ordering date and the day is a default. The coordinate is a general Astoria point, not a parcel.
stops.campa: A government salary well above the ordinary, plus private code-consulting income, makes him for a few years a man with money to place. He puts it into Queens property through Cody Realty: lots and houses in Astoria, Woodside, Jackson Heights, all of it leveraged. The bureau's appropriation is shrinking at the same time and the cover firm's commercial business is thinning. The New York property market turns down before the stock market does. By the autumn of 1929 the bureau and the investments are both gone, within months of each other.

stops.name: The State Department, the bureau closed
stops.date_confidence: attested: Wikipedia gives 31 October 1929 as the closure after Secretary Henry L. Stimson withdrew State Department support. The pool's geography lens dated the same event 1 November 1929, contradicting its own chronology and its own source; 31 October is used. The Stimson line is [A] and its earlier [R] tag is dropped: it is printed in Henry L. Stimson and McGeorge Bundy, On Active Service in Peace and War (1948), p. 188, as reported speech, 'as he later said'. It does not appear anywhere in Yardley's own book. That the 1929 shutdown was a longer Army reorganization compressed into a Stimson legend is [R], from Kahn.
stops.campa: The Secretary of State is shown a sheaf of decoded Japanese traffic and withdraws the State Department's share of the money. On the thirty-first of October the New York office is shut, its files packed off to the Army and its people let go into an economy that had collapsed two days before. Yardley is forty and holds the only detailed knowledge in America of an operation that officially never existed. Stimson's reason, given nineteen years later in his memoirs, is a rule of conduct between gentlemen. Nobody records him saying it in 1929, and it is nowhere in Yardley's own book.
stops.quote: Gentlemen do not read each other's mail.
stops.quote_source: Henry L. Stimson, recalled in Henry L. Stimson and McGeorge Bundy, On Active Service in Peace and War (Harper & Brothers, 1948), p. 188
suggested_refs: Stimson and Bundy, On Active Service in Peace and War (1948), p. 188, the earliest located printing of the line

stops.name: Worthington, home with nothing
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The return to Worthington seeking consulting and teaching work, and the brief association with the Northwestern University Scientific Crime Detection Laboratory in Chicago around 1930, are both the pool's, from Kahn and the Hannah NSA study, unconfirmed by anything fetched here. December 1929 is an ordering date and the day is a default. The Chicago laboratory is folded into this stop rather than given a placeholder pin of its own.
stops.campa: He goes back to the town that suspended him, out of work at forty, with a wife, a son and property debts. There is consulting that does not come and teaching that does not come, and a short association with the Northwestern University crime detection laboratory in Chicago, where he offers instruction in decoding. Nothing holds. He has one asset left that is entirely his own: eleven years of reading other governments' mail, and no law on the books forbidding him to describe it.

stops.name: Indianapolis, Bobbs-Merrill publishes the book
stops.date_confidence: attested as to year and publisher: en.wikipedia, 'The American Black Chamber', gives 1931, The Bobbs-Merrill Company, 375 pages, and Wikipedia's Yardley article carries the sales figures used here. The pool's precise date of 1 June 1931 is not supported by anything fetched and is downgraded to the year; the day is a default. The Saturday Evening Post excerpts are [R], unconfirmed. The coordinate is a general downtown Indianapolis point, not a verified Bobbs-Merrill address. Friedman's damage assessment and Kahn's contrary finding are both [R], from the pool.
stops.campa: Bobbs-Merrill of Indianapolis publishes The American Black Chamber, and the operation Washington had never admitted to is in the shop windows with its methods, its successes and its Japanese solutions named. It sells 17,931 copies in the United States, 5,480 in Britain, and 33,119 in Japan, where it is read as a confession. The State Department disavows the disclosures. William Friedman files a grave damage assessment; Kahn, decades later, finds no worldwide blackout of codes that followed. Both judgments are still in the file.
stops.quote: The Background? The Black Chamber. The Cryptographic Bureau, where specialists pore over cipher telegrams of foreign governments, where chemists forge diplomatic seals and photograph letters of foreign plenipotentiaries.
stops.quote_source: Herbert O. Yardley, The American Black Chamber (Bobbs-Merrill, 1931), Foreword

stops.name: New York, the marshals at the publisher's office
stops.date_confidence: the seizure is [A]: Wikipedia, verbatim, 'Yardley's second book, Japanese Diplomatic Codes: 1921-1922, was seized by U.S. marshals and never published. The manuscript was declassified in 1979.' The date of 20 February, the venue at Macmillan and MacArthur's intervention are all [R], the pool's, unconfirmed here; the coordinate is consistent with Macmillan's Fifth Avenue premises but unverified. The title varies between sources: Wikipedia has 'Japanese Diplomatic Codes: 1921-1922', the pool 'Japanese Diplomatic Secrets, 1921-1922'. The statute is [A]: 48 Stat. 122, ch. 57, enacted 10 June 1933, per the US House Office of the Law Revision Counsel annotation to 18 U.S.C. 952. It postdates the seizure by nearly four months, so it cannot have been the instrument of it; the pool's afterlife lens states the causation backwards and is corrected here.
stops.campa: United States marshals come to his publisher and take the manuscript of his second book, on the Japanese diplomatic codes of 1921 and 1922. It is never published in his lifetime; it goes into a vault for forty-six years. In June, four months after the seizure, Congress makes it a crime to publish diplomatic codes or anything obtained by cryptanalysis, a statute the newspapers call the Yardley law. It cannot touch him, his book having come first. The sources do not agree even on what the seized manuscript was called: Japanese Diplomatic Codes in one, Japanese Diplomatic Secrets in another.

stops.name: Washington, the finger
stops.date_confidence: [R]. The laboratory accident, the infection and the amputation on 21 May 1933 are the pool's, from Kahn, and no source fetched this session confirms them. The place of the accident is not established anywhere reached, so the coordinate is a general Washington point.
stops.campa: Compounding a secret ink for one of the schemes he now lives on, he cuts his right palm. The cut goes septic. A finger is amputated on the twenty-first of May. The hand that took the House cable apart in two hours is short a finger at forty-four, and the man is writing detective novels, ghost work and film treatments to keep a household running.
